name.text: L1-Q01 — Diagnosing absolute instability from a sounding

questiontext.text: A 12:00 UTC sounding over an inland station shows the temperature decreasing at 11 °C/km through the lowest 2 km, with the parcel unsaturated throughout that layer. Which best describes the stability of this layer?

generalfeedback.text: Rationale: The environmental lapse rate (11 °C/km) exceeds the dry adiabatic lapse rate (9.8 °C/km), so an unsaturated parcel displaced upward becomes warmer than its surroundings and continues to rise. This is the definition of absolute instability. Conditional instability requires the environmental lapse rate to fall between the dry and saturated adiabatic rates (DALR > ELR > SALR) — not the case here, where the ELR exceeds even the DALR.

name.text: L1-Q02 — Forecasting afternoon convection from a morning sounding

questiontext.text: A morning sounding shows a conditionally unstable layer between 850 and 500 hPa, with a shallow surface-based inversion below 950 hPa and a lifted condensation level near 870 hPa. Surface heating is expected to add 6 °C through the afternoon. No significant moisture advection is forecast. What is the most operationally appropriate afternoon forecast?

generalfeedback.text: Rationale: Six degrees of surface heating will erode the shallow morning inversion, allowing surface parcels to reach the LCL near 870 hPa and tap into the conditionally unstable layer above. Conditional instability means that once saturated, a parcel continues to rise — so convection initiation is favored. Forecasting "no convection" because the morning is stable misreads the diurnal evolution. Forecasting "widespread severe weather" overstates what conditional instability alone supports without additional information about shear or moisture depth.

answer.text: Isolated to scattered convection developing after the morning inversion erodes.
No convection — the morning inversion will suppress vertical motion all day.
A stratocumulus deck capped at the LCL with no precipitation.
